title: THE BIBLE GETS STRANGER THE MORE YOU READ IT—AND THE STRANGEST PART IS HOW EVERY STORY EXPOSES SOMETHING ABOUT YOU
paragraphs: THE BIBLE GETS STRANGER THE MORE YOU READ IT—AND THE STRANGEST PART IS HOW EVERY STORY EXPOSES SOMETHING ABOUT YOU

Talking donkeys. Golden tumors. A man wrestling through the night. A face shining with unbearable glory. A bronze serpent lifted above dying people. These are not embarrassing stories Christians need to explain away. They are ancient testimonies that confront our assumptions about God, sin, judgment, mercy, and the astonishing way Scripture ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
There is a moment that happens to people who actually begin reading the Bible for themselves.
Not just opening it to find a comforting verse.
Not just listening to their favorite preacher explain the passages everyone already knows.
Not just reading the parts that look beautiful on a coffee mug.
I mean really reading it.

Page after page. Chapter after chapter. Through the genealogies, the blood, the battles, the laws, the miracles, the betrayals, the strange visions, the uncomfortable judgments, and the moments when God does something so unexpected that you have to stop and stare at the page.
And somewhere along the way, a thought begins forming.
Wait. That's actually in the Bible?
A donkey talks.
People make golden images of tumors.
A man wrestles with a mysterious figure until sunrise and walks away limping.
Another man comes down a mountain with a face so radiant that people are afraid to approach him.
God tells Moses to lift a bronze serpent on a pole so dying Israelites can look at it and live.
And perhaps the most unsettling discovery of all?
The Bible does not always stop to satisfy our curiosity.
Sometimes it leaves us standing in the mystery.
Sometimes it tells us exactly what happened without explaining every detail of how.
And sometimes, hundreds of years later, another passage opens a window into an earlier story so suddenly that everything you thought you understood begins to change.
But here is where this becomes personal.
Because if you stay with Scripture long enough, you begin to realize that its strangest stories are not merely about strange things that happened to other people.
They confront the blindness we refuse to acknowledge.
The pride we have learned to disguise.
The shame we keep carrying.
The wounds we cannot explain.
The idols we have polished until they look respectable.
And the desperate human need for a Savior who can do what no human being can accomplish.
You may open the Bible expecting to examine its stories.
But there will be moments when you feel as though its stories are examining you.
And one of the first places this happens is on a lonely road, where a man who believed he could see spiritually was about to be corrected by an animal.
Yes.
An actual donkey.
In Numbers 22, Balaam is traveling with Moabite officials after being summoned by King Balak, who wants Israel cursed.

Balaam has received permission to go under specific conditions, yet God's anger is kindled as he travels. The passage does not explain every dimension of that tension, but it does make one thing painfully clear: Balaam's journey is not spiritually safe.
The angel of the LORD stands in the road with a drawn sword.
Balaam does not see him.
His donkey does.
The animal turns aside.
Balaam strikes her.
The donkey presses against a wall to avoid the angel, crushing Balaam's foot.
He strikes her again.
Finally, the donkey lies down beneath him.
And Balaam, furious, beats her with his staff.
Then comes one of the most extraordinary sentences in the Old Testament.
Numbers 22:28 says:
וַיִּפְתַּח יְהוָה אֶת־פִּי הָאָתוֹן
Vayyiftaḥ YHWH et-pi ha'aton.
“And the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey.”
The Hebrew does not merely suggest that Balaam imagined the animal speaking. The narrative explicitly attributes the opening of her mouth to the LORD.
And the donkey asks Balaam what she has done to deserve being struck three times.
Even more astonishingly, Balaam answers her.
Think about that.
The man is so consumed with anger that he enters into an argument with a talking donkey.
Then God opens Balaam's eyes.
He sees the angel.
The drawn sword.
The danger he could not perceive.
And suddenly, the entire scene changes.
The animal he was beating had been protecting him.
The creature he considered beneath him had seen what he could not.
The one who believed himself spiritually knowledgeable was exposed as spiritually blind.
And the donkey had been right.
How many times have we mistaken God's interruption for an inconvenience?
How many times have we become angry because something blocked our plans, never considering that the obstacle might be protecting us from a danger we cannot see?
That does not mean every delay, disappointment, or closed door is a supernatural warning. Scripture does not give us permission to interpret every frustration that way.
But Balaam's story does warn us that religious knowledge does not guarantee spiritual discernment.
A person can speak about God and still resist His correction.
A person can be gifted and still be dangerously wrong.
A person can recognize the language of heaven while remaining attached to the rewards of earth.
The New Testament later warns about Balaam's greed and corrupt influence (2 Peter 2:15–16; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14).
So this is not merely a charming story about an animal with a voice.
It is a warning about the human heart.
And if that makes you uncomfortable, keep reading.
Because the next story is even harder to imagine.
In 1 Samuel 4–6, Israel suffers a devastating defeat at the hands of the Philistines.
The ark of the covenant is captured.

The ark was associated with God's covenant presence among His people. But Israel had treated it as though possessing a sacred object could guarantee victory even when their relationship with God was profoundly disordered.
And when the Philistines capture it, they bring it into the temple of their god, Dagon.
The following morning, Dagon's statue is found fallen on its face before the ark.
They set it upright.
The next morning, it has fallen again, this time with its head and hands broken off.
The message is unmistakable.
The LORD cannot be reduced to a captured religious trophy.
The Philistines then experience severe affliction.

The Hebrew text describes the swellings with the word עֳפָלִים (ofalim), commonly translated as tumors or swellings. The exact medical condition is debated, and some textual traditions use a different Hebrew term. We should not pretend to know the precise diagnosis.
But the affliction is serious.
The people are terrified.
And when the Philistines finally decide to return the ark, their priests and diviners advise them to send a guilt offering.
Five golden tumors.
Five golden mice.
Yes, you read that correctly.
Golden representations of their afflictions and of mice associated with the devastation of their land.
First Samuel 6:4–5 records this unusual offering.
And before someone rushes to turn this into a universal spiritual formula, notice something important.
These instructions come from Philistine religious advisers, not from a direct divine command prescribing how God's people should worship.
The narrative reports what they did. It does not establish golden replicas of diseases as a biblical pattern of repentance.
That distinction matters.
Not everything recorded in Scripture is something Scripture commands us to imitate.
The Bible is truthful enough to show us human beings acting with fear, confusion, superstition, arrogance, and partial understanding.
And in this particular account, God's supremacy over Dagon and the Philistines becomes impossible to ignore.
Their idol cannot even stand upright.
Their attempts to control the ark fail.
The God of Israel is not defeated simply because Israel has suffered defeat.
And there is a warning here for every generation.
We can carry religious objects.
Use religious language.
Wear religious clothing.
Display religious symbols.
Attend religious gatherings.
And still misunderstand the living God.
The ark was never meant to replace obedience to the LORD.
And our Christian identity is never meant to replace genuine trust in Jesus Christ.
A cross around your neck is not a substitute for following the One who died upon a cross.
A Bible sitting beside your bed is not the same as allowing its truth to shape your life.
A Christian label cannot save a soul.
Only Christ can.
And now Scripture takes us somewhere quieter.
Not into a pagan temple.
Not onto a dangerous road.
But beside a river, in the darkness, with a frightened man who is about to encounter God in a way he will never forget.
His name is Jacob.
And if you have ever tried to outrun your past, you may recognize something of yourself in him.
Jacob's life has been tangled in conflict, deception, fear, family rivalry, and the consequences of his own choices.
Now, in Genesis 32, he is preparing to meet his brother Esau.
The brother he had wronged.
The brother whose anger he once feared.
Jacob sends his family and possessions across the stream.
And he remains alone.
Genesis 32:24 says:
וַיֵּאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ עַד עֲלוֹת הַשָּׁחַר
Vayye'aveq ish immo ad alot hashachar.
“And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day.”
A man.
That is how the encounter begins.
But the identity of this mysterious wrestler becomes increasingly profound.
The stranger touches Jacob's hip, dislocating it.
Jacob refuses to release him without a blessing.
And then comes the question.
“What is your name?”
“Jacob.”
The man who had spent so much of his life grasping, maneuvering, and struggling must speak his own name.
Then the stranger gives him another.
Israel.
Genesis 32:28 connects that name with Jacob's struggle with God and with men.
The precise linguistic derivation of the name Israel is discussed by scholars, but the narrative itself clearly emphasizes Jacob's struggle with God.
Jacob names the place Peniel, saying that he has seen God face to face and yet his life has been preserved.
Hosea 12:3–4 later recalls this encounter and refers to the mysterious opponent as an angel.
The biblical texts therefore invite us to recognize a genuine divine encounter while leaving questions about its exact manifestation.
Some Christian interpreters understand the event as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. Others understand it as an encounter with God mediated through an angelic figure.
Scripture does not explicitly identify the wrestler as Jesus, and we should not turn a possible interpretation into an unquestionable fact.
But the theological significance remains astonishing.
Jacob receives a blessing.
He receives a new name.
And he walks away limping.
The encounter that changes his identity also changes the way he walks.
There is something deeply moving about that.
We often imagine that if God truly touches our lives, every visible sign of struggle should disappear.
Every consequence erased.
Every scar removed.
Every painful memory forgotten.
But Jacob's story does not give us that simplistic picture.
He is blessed.
And he limps.
He has encountered God.
And his hip still hurts.
He has a new name.
And he still must face Esau.
God's blessing does not remove his responsibility to confront the past.
Perhaps you know what it is like to love God while still carrying the consequences of choices you regret.
Perhaps you have repented, yet there are relationships that remain complicated.
Perhaps forgiveness has been offered, yet trust still needs rebuilding.
Perhaps you have experienced God's mercy without receiving an immediate escape from every painful circumstance.
Jacob's limp reminds us that transformation is not always the absence of weakness.
Sometimes grace changes how we live with weakness.
And in the New Testament, Paul would hear the Lord say, “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV).
That is not a promise that every wound will remain.
It is a promise that Christ's grace is sufficient even when weakness remains.
And that is good news for people who have spent years pretending to be stronger than they are.
But the Bible is not finished surprising us.
Because there is another man who encounters God, and this time the evidence is written across his face.
Moses has been on Mount Sinai in the presence of the LORD.
When he descends carrying the tablets of the testimony, something extraordinary has happened.
His face is shining.
Exodus 34:29 uses a form of the Hebrew verb קָרַן (qaran), describing the radiance of the skin of his face.

The Hebrew wording is striking because the root is related to a word for horn. This linguistic connection contributed to the famous older Latin rendering that influenced artistic depictions of Moses with horns.
But the narrative's context is clear.
Moses' face is radiating because he has been speaking with God.
Aaron and the Israelites are afraid to come near him.
Moses speaks to them and later uses a veil.
Imagine standing before someone whose face visibly bears the effects of an encounter with the holy God.
No stage lighting.
No theatrical performance.
No human technique.
Just a man who has been in God's presence.
Yet the most remarkable explanation comes much later.
In 2 Corinthians 3, Paul reflects on Moses' veil and the glory associated with the old covenant.
He contrasts that glory with the surpassing glory of the ministry of the Spirit under the new covenant.
And then he writes in 2 Corinthians 3:18:
The Greek word translated “changed” is μεταμορφούμεθα (metamorphoumetha).
It describes being transformed.
Not merely appearing different.
Not learning to perform religious behavior more convincingly.
Being transformed.
Paul is not promising that every Christian's face will physically glow.
He is describing the Spirit's transforming work as believers behold the Lord's glory.
And in the next chapter, Paul identifies the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).
This is where the story reaches into our lives.
We spend enormous amounts of energy trying to change ourselves through image management.
We curate appearances.
Hide weaknesses.
Measure ourselves against other people.
And sometimes even turn Christianity into another exhausting performance.
But the Gospel does not begin with a demand that sinners manufacture their own glory.
It announces Jesus Christ, through whom God gives light to hearts that could never produce it themselves.
The transformation is real.
The Spirit works within us.
And the glory belongs to God.
Yet of all the strange stories we have considered, there is one that Jesus Himself explicitly brings into the center of His explanation of salvation.
And this is where the entire journey becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because it involves dying people.
Deadly serpents.
A bronze image lifted on a pole.
And a Savior who would one day be lifted up on a cross.
In Numbers 21, the Israelites speak against God and Moses.
Their complaint exposes the bitterness and unbelief that have taken root during their wilderness journey.
Then fiery serpents come among the people.
Many are bitten.
Many die.
The people confess their sin and ask Moses to pray.
And the LORD gives an extraordinary instruction.
Moses is to make a fiery serpent and set it upon a pole.
Those who are bitten are to look at it and live.
Numbers 21:9 says:
וְהִבִּיט אֶל־נְחַשׁ הַנְּחֹשֶׁת וָחָי
Vehibbit el-neḥash hanneḥoshet vaḥay.
“And when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.” (KJV)
The Hebrew contains a memorable wordplay between naḥash (serpent) and neḥoshet (bronze or copper).
But the theological point is not that bronze possesses supernatural healing power.
The healing comes through God's merciful provision, received according to His word.
And this is important because centuries later, in 2 Kings 18:4, King Hezekiah destroys the bronze serpent after the Israelites begin burning incense to it.
They had turned a former instrument of God's provision into an object of idolatrous devotion.
Think about that.
Something God once used for good had become something people worshiped instead of God.
Even a sacred reminder can become an idol when it receives the devotion that belongs to the LORD alone.
But the most important revelation about the bronze serpent does not come from Hezekiah.
It comes from Jesus.
In John 3, Jesus is speaking with Nicodemus, a Pharisee and teacher of Israel.
Nicodemus is trying to understand the necessity of being born again.
And Jesus reaches back into the wilderness.
John 3:14–15 says:
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus Himself connects the bronze serpent with His coming crucifixion.
The Israelites were dying and could not heal themselves.
God provided a means by which they could live.
And Jesus uses that historical event to illuminate the salvation He came to accomplish.
The comparison does not mean Jesus was sinful or evil like the serpent imagery might suggest.
Scripture explicitly teaches that Christ was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
Rather, Jesus identifies a God-given pattern of deliverance: those facing death receive life through the provision God has appointed.
The cross is not an accident.
It is not simply an inspirational example of sacrificial love.
It is the place where the sinless Son of God gives Himself for sinners.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Galatians 3:13 declares that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.
And Isaiah 53 speaks of the suffering Servant who bears the iniquities of many.
Now consider the original scene again.
Imagine an Israelite lying in the dust.
The venom has entered his body.
His strength is failing.
He cannot negotiate with the poison.
He cannot reverse the bite through sheer determination.
He cannot earn a cure by promising to become a better person tomorrow.
But God has provided a way to live.
And Jesus says that this event points toward something far greater.
A world wounded by sin.
Human beings unable to rescue themselves.
And the Son of God lifted up so that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life.
Then comes the verse that countless people have memorized, often without remembering the strange wilderness story immediately preceding it.
John 3:16.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” (KJV)
Do you see it now?
The talking donkey exposes spiritual blindness.
The golden tumors appear in a narrative demonstrating that the LORD cannot be controlled or defeated by idols.
Jacob's wrestling reveals the mystery of divine blessing in the life of a deeply flawed man.
Moses' radiant face becomes part of Paul's explanation of the surpassing glory of the new covenant.
And the bronze serpent becomes an image Jesus Himself uses to explain His saving work.
These passages do not all function in exactly the same way.
Not every detail is a hidden prophecy.
Not every unusual event is a coded reference to the crucifixion.
Not every biblical character is a secret symbol of Jesus.
Faithful reading requires us to respect what each passage actually says, its historical setting, its literary context, and the way later Scripture interprets it.
But taken together within the Bible's unfolding story, they reveal a consistent truth.
Human beings are more spiritually needy than we want to admit.
And God is more merciful than we could ever deserve.
There is another detail about the Bible that should change how we read it.
Its stories are not arranged to make its human characters look consistently admirable.
Abraham fears.
Jacob deceives.
Moses disobeys.
David commits adultery and arranges a man's death.
Peter denies knowing Jesus.
The disciples argue about greatness.
And Paul openly remembers that he once persecuted the church.
Scripture does not protect its heroes from the truth about themselves.
Why?
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of impressive people earning God's approval through flawless lives.
It is the story of the holy God acting in creation, covenant, judgment, mercy, and redemption, culminating in Jesus Christ.
That does not excuse the sins of its characters.
It makes God's grace all the more astonishing.
And perhaps this is why certain biblical stories feel so uncomfortable.
They destroy the illusion that spiritual maturity is the same as maintaining a spotless public image.
They remind us that religious people can be blind.
That gifted people can be greedy.
That wounded people can be changed.
That sacred things can become idols.
And that sinners need more than inspiration.
They need redemption.
Now, perhaps you have been reading all of this with a quiet question rising inside you.
What does any of this have to do with me?
Maybe more than you expected.
Because there are people reading these words who have become very good at looking spiritually healthy while privately struggling.
You know how to say “God is good.”
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which Bible verses to share.
You know how to encourage everyone else.
But there are things you have not told anyone.
A habit you keep returning to.
A relationship you damaged.
A resentment you keep feeding.
A private compromise you keep defending.
A prayer you have almost stopped praying because the answer has taken so long.
Or a kind of spiritual exhaustion that makes you wonder whether you are still growing at all.
And perhaps you have begun to believe that your failures are the truest thing about you.
But listen carefully.
Your sin must not be minimized.
Your wounds must not be mocked.
Your responsibility must not be denied.
And God's grace must not be reduced to permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not come merely to make us feel better about the darkness.
He came to save us from sin and bring us into the light.
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), referring to a change of mind or heart that, in biblical usage, involves turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness through emotional suffering.
It is not pretending your past never happened.
It is not manufacturing enough tears to convince God that you deserve another chance.
It is turning to God in response to His truth and mercy.
Mark 1:15 records Jesus proclaiming:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
Repent.
And believe.
Not because your repentance makes the cross effective.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is the Savior in whom forgiveness and new life are found.
And if you have fallen again, the answer is not to hide deeper.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not our works, while also affirming that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not mean sin is harmless.
Grace means sin does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
This is the heart of the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because the damage never mattered.
Not because everyone you hurt is required to trust you immediately.
Not because repentance guarantees the removal of every earthly consequence.
But because the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ make forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and genuine transformation possible.
He does not rewrite history by pretending evil was good.
He redeems sinners without calling their sin righteous.
He gives a new future without requiring us to deny the truth about the past.
And He is still changing lives.
Maybe yours is one of them.
There is something else I want you to notice before you leave this article.
When Jesus rose from the dead, He did not tell His disciples to build a movement around the strangest stories in the Bible.
He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.
Luke 24:27 tells us that beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Jesus explained the things concerning Himself in the Scriptures.
And Luke 24:44–47 connects the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms with His suffering, resurrection, and the proclamation of repentance for the forgiveness of sins in His name.
That is the destination.
Not fascination without faith.
Not mystery without obedience.
Not knowledge without love.
Not biblical trivia that makes us feel intellectually superior to people who have never studied Hebrew or Greek.
The goal is to know the living God through Jesus Christ.
To read His Word carefully.
To receive His truth humbly.
To repent where we have sinned.
To trust His grace.
And to follow Him with lives increasingly shaped by His Spirit.
The original biblical languages are precious because they help us understand what the biblical authors communicated.
But knowing Hebrew does not automatically make a person holy.
Understanding Greek does not guarantee obedience.
And being able to explain a talking donkey is not the same as listening when God corrects your own heart.
The question is not merely whether you can understand the strange passages.
The deeper question is whether you will allow the truth of Scripture to challenge the comfortable stories you have been telling yourself.
Maybe you have been like Balaam, angry at an interruption while refusing to examine your direction.
Maybe you have been like Jacob, afraid of facing the consequences of your past.
Maybe you have become so attached to a religious symbol, personality, tradition, or institution that you have lost sight of the God it was supposed to direct you toward.
Maybe you have been trying to manufacture a spiritual glow while neglecting the quiet work of prayer, repentance, Scripture, and obedience.
Or maybe you feel like one of those dying Israelites.
Exhausted.
Guilty.
Unable to save yourself.
And desperately needing mercy.
If that is you, do not turn this into another moment of religious performance.
Turn to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess the sin you have been defending.
Ask for mercy.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And take the next faithful step.
Sometimes that step is apologizing.
Sometimes it is ending a sinful relationship or pattern.
Sometimes it is seeking pastoral counsel or wise Christian support.
Sometimes it is opening your Bible again after months of silence.
Sometimes it is choosing to forgive while still establishing necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it is simply praying, “Lord Jesus, have mercy on me. Teach me to follow You.”
And if your faith feels weak, remember that the strength of salvation is not found in how impressive you can make your faith appear.
It is found in the Savior upon whom faith depends.
Be honest.
Which of these stories reached the part of your heart you have been avoiding?
Was it Balaam's blindness?
Jacob's limp?
The warning against turning sacred things into idols?
Moses' encounter with God's glory?
Or the bronze serpent pointing toward Christ?
If you are still fighting to follow Jesus through a difficult season, you can simply comment, “I'm still fighting.”
If you need encouragement and prayer, comment, “Pray for me.”
And if this article has reminded you that your past does not have to define your future in Christ, comment, “Jesus is still changing me.”
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
Not merely to increase its reach.
And perhaps, through that unexpected beginning, they will encounter the truth about the crucified and risen Savior.
Because the deeper you go into Scripture, the more you discover how much there is still to learn.
And this is why the Gospel Warrior ministry exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to sell you salvation.
Not to make you dependent on a personality.
But to encourage you to grow in biblical understanding, deepen your relationship with Christ, and become more grounded in the truth of God's Word.
These resources are intended to help people study, pray, understand the Gospel, and mature in their walk with God.
And if this ministry has encouraged you, taught you something, or helped you return to Scripture, I want to extend a personal invitation.
You do not have to pay for God's favor.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not pressure.
These products are not spiritual necessities.
They do not make anyone more saved, more loved by God, or more deserving of His grace.
You can still read.
Still learn.
Still pray.
Still share.
Still make use of the free resources.
And above all, still grow in Christ.
Because the Gospel is not a product.
Jesus Christ is not behind a paywall.
Salvation is the free gift of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
It does not purchase the mercy of God.
That distinction is not a small detail.
It is part of remaining faithful to the very Gospel we are trying to proclaim.
And perhaps that is the most important lesson hidden in plain sight throughout these astonishing biblical accounts.
God does not need our attempts to make Him more marketable.
He does not need us to remove the uncomfortable passages.
He does not need us to exaggerate the miracles.
He does not need us to manufacture secret meanings the biblical authors never intended.
He calls us to receive His Word with reverence, study it faithfully, and proclaim Jesus Christ truthfully.
Because the Bible is already astonishing.
A donkey speaks because God opens its mouth.
A pagan idol falls because it cannot stand before the living God.
A frightened patriarch wrestles through the night and receives a new name.
A prophet's face shines after speaking with the LORD.
A bronze serpent is lifted in the wilderness, and centuries later Jesus declares that the Son of Man must likewise be lifted up.
And at the center of the Christian faith stands the greatest wonder of all.
The eternal Son of God took on human flesh.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed sinners without approving their sin.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He healed the broken.
He bore the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Not as a metaphor for positive thinking.
Not as a symbol that life sometimes gets better.
But as the risen Lord whose victory over sin and death stands at the heart of the apostolic Gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And because He lives, repentance is not hopeless.
Forgiveness is not imaginary.
Transformation is not merely self-improvement.
And death does not have the final word for those who belong to Him.
So read the strange passages.
Ask the difficult questions.
Study the original languages when you can.
Pay attention to the context.
Refuse interpretations that sound exciting but cannot be supported by Scripture.
Let the difficult stories humble you.
Let the judgments sober you.
Let the promises strengthen you.
Let the cross expose both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable greatness of divine love.
And let the resurrection remind you that the God who raised Jesus from the dead is not finished accomplishing His purposes.
You may have come here because the Bible contains a talking donkey.
But I pray you leave thinking about the Savior who speaks life to sinners.
You may have come because golden tumors sounded unbelievable.
But I pray you leave with a greater reverence for the God who cannot be controlled by human idols.
You may have come because a man wrestled with God and walked away limping.
But I pray you leave knowing that your weakness does not place you beyond the reach of His grace.
And you may have come because a bronze serpent sounded strange.
But I pray you leave looking to the One who was lifted up for our salvation.
Because one day, the strangest thing about your story may not be what happened to you.

It may be that after everything you did, everything you lost, everything you feared, and everything you thought could never be redeemed, Jesus Christ met you with mercy, called you to repentance, and began making you new.

The miracle is not that God can make a donkey speak, or a man's face shine. The miracle that should bring us to our knees is that the holy God still calls sinners out of darkness and into the life of His beloved Son.
